newsitem.title: USA: Kaiser Permanente, unions unveil cooperative pact.
newsitem.headline: Kaiser Permanente, unions unveil cooperative pact.

text.p: Kaiser Permanente and its unions Thursday unveiled a far-reaching cooperative plan that would make it labour's health plan of choice, while boosting the job security and decision-making power of its workers.

Leaders of Kaiser, the country's largest non-profit health care system, and a multi-union group representing more than 50,000 of its workers, said the labour-management partnership was a response to what they called pressure to cut health care quality from for-profit health maintenance organisations.

"We realise that we set the standard in the health care industry and we are going to be far more successful if we work together," Kaiser Chief Executive Officer Dr. David Lawrence said in a telephone news conference late Thursday.

"Our unions have come to this point because we are deeply concerned about an industry in which for-profit HMOs are driving down patient care standards and forcing Kaiser, a non-profit HMO, to compete with managed care providers that see a dollar spent on patient care as a dollar diverted from profits," added Kathy Schmidt, president of the Oregon Federation of Nurses and Health Professionals.

The proposal, which must be ratified by a majority of the union members it would cover, would be one of the country's largest labour-management partnerships and the first on a nationwide scale in the health care industry.

It would join a relative handful of other such cooperative agreements, including those between the United Auto Workers and General Motors Corp.'s Saturn division, the Union of Needletrades, Industrial and Textile Employees, and Levi Strauss & Co., the United Steelworkers of American and National Steel Corp. and the Communications Workers of America and Nynex Corp.

Like most of the agreements, the Kaiser deal would give frontline workers and their unions influence over management decisions in areas such as marketing and patient care through joint committees at various levels of the hierarchy.

"Kaiser has agreed that we're going to be involved right at the very top of the decison-making process," said chief union negotiator Peter diCicco, president of the AFL-CIO's Industrial Union Department.
By involving frontline workers in decisions, officials of both sides said, Kaiser will be able to compete with HMOs on quality of care, instead of on cost alone.

"By not working in in concert, we literally give an advantage to our competitors, who do not share our goals and our philosophy," said Dr. Oliver Goldsmith, president of the Southern California Permanente Medical Group.

Under the deal, Oakland, Calif.-based Kaiser, which has 7.8 million members in 18 states, would be backed by the AFL-CIO, whose 78 unions have 13.1 million members, as a union-endorsed health care provider. The backing could be especially helpful to Kaiser in medical plans that are jointly administered by union and management representatives.

The deal gives Kaiser's union employees greater job security and a promise that it will remain neutral in union organising campaigns and accept union representation where a majority of workers have signed cards, instead of insisting on elections that can be drawn out and contentious.
Leaders of the Service Employees International Union, which represents 29,000 of the Kaiser workers, urged their members to approve the deal.
AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said the partnershp would not affect the stances of unions that are currently in difficult contract talks with Kaiser in Denver and Oakland.
Sweeney, known for his aggressive, confrontational organising tactics, said he whole-heartedly supported the cooperative arrangement with Kaiser.
"I've often said that you have to build bridges and occasionally you have to block a few bridges," he said. "I see this as an opportunity to build bridges."
